Materials

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
We address the challenge of Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning (FSCIL) specifically applied to 3D point cloud segmentation. Current approaches predominantly rely on Euclidean embedding spaces, which are suboptimal for representing the complex, latent hierarchical structures intrinsic to 3D data. Furthermore, in an incremental setting where new classes must be learned from scarce data (few-shot), standard methods suffer severely from the "stability-plasticity" trade-off. They lack the embedding capacity to accommodate new classes without distorting previously learned representations, leading to significant catastrophic forgetting and overfitting.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that projecting point cloud features into a hyperbolic embedding space (specifically the Poincaré model) will naturally mitigate catastrophic forgetting due to the space's exponential volume expansion and negative curvature. We believe that by establishing "Ideal Prototypes"—fixed, distinct anchors positioned at the asymptotic boundary of the hyperbolic space—we can enforce a stable feature-classifier alignment. This structure should allow the model to reserve ample embedding volume for future classes while preserving the structural hierarchy of existing knowledge, effectively solving the data scarcity and interference problems inherent to FSCIL.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)
We propose a framework named **HiPo (Hyperbolic Ideal Prototypes Optimization)**. The approach avoids dynamic classifier updates (which lead to drift) in favor of a fixed geometric structure.

1.  **Ideal Prototype Initialization:**
    Instead of randomly initializing or learning classifier weights, we will pre-assign "Ideal Prototypes" on the boundary of the Poincaré ball (representing points at infinity). To ensure these positions are semantically meaningful, we will utilize a frozen language model (like CLIP) to encode class names. These text embeddings will guide the relative positioning of prototypes on the manifold—ensuring semantically similar classes are closer—while enforcing orthogonality to maximize the discriminative margin between distinct classes.

2.  **Hyperbolic Projection:**
    We will employ a standard 3D point cloud backbone to extract Euclidean features, which will then be mapped onto the hyperbolic manifold using an exponential map. A hyperbolic feed-forward layer (Mobius layer) will process these features to align them with the geometric constraints of the space.

3.  **Busemann-Based Optimization:**
    Since our targets (Ideal Prototypes) lie at infinity, standard geodesic distance calculations are intractable. We will implement a loss function based on the **Busemann function**, which provides a mathematically rigorous way to measure the "distance" to a point at infinity. This will pull sample embeddings toward their respective class prototypes at the boundary.

4.  **Uncertainty-Aware Regularization:**
    To prevent overfitting on the few-shot examples (where the model might rush points to the boundary too quickly), we will incorporate an uncertainty penalty. We will use the hyperbolic distance of a sample from the origin as a proxy for certainty. By penalizing this distance during early adaptation, we aim to maintain a "safe" margin and prevent vanishing gradients, ensuring the model remains plastic enough to accept new information without collapsing the feature space.

## Expected Contribution
This research expects to demonstrate that hyperbolic geometry provides a superior inductive bias for 3D point cloud segmentation compared to Euclidean spaces. Theoretically, we aim to formalize the use of Busemann functions for optimization against infinite prototypes in a dense segmentation task. Practically, this approach should yield a rehearsal-free incremental learning system that significantly reduces catastrophic forgetting and generalizes well to novel classes with minimal supervision.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated a novel framework, Hyperbolic Ideal Prototypes Optimization (HiPo), for Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning (FSCIL) in 3D point cloud segmentation.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **S3DIS:** Large-scale colored 3D point clouds of indoor spaces. Used for both in-domain and cross-dataset evaluation.
    *   **ScanNetv2:** Large-scale colored 3D point clouds of indoor spaces. Used for both in-domain and cross-dataset evaluation.
    *   **Cross-Dataset Setup:** Transition from ScanNetv2 (Base) to S3DIS (Incremental). Ten classes from ScanNetv2 were used as the base, and eight new classes from S3DIS were introduced in incremental sessions. The label spaces were strictly disjoint.

*   **Experimental Settings (Splits):**
    *   **S3DIS:** Evaluated on 4-3T (4 base classes, 3 incremental tasks), 7-3T, and 10-3T settings.
    *   **ScanNetv2:** Evaluated on 10-2T, 10-5T, and 15-5T settings.
    *   **Shot Count:** primarily 5-shot (5 labeled samples per new class). Sensitivity analysis was conducted from 1-shot up to full-data.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **Last:** The accuracy (mIoU) after the final task.
    *   **AIA (Average Incremental Accuracy):** The average accuracy across all tasks learned sequentially.
    *   **F_Last (Average Forgetting Rate):** Measures performance decline on learned tasks after adapting to the last task (lower is better).
    *   **mIoU:** Mean Intersection-over-Union used for segmentation performance.
    *   **Dunn Index:** Used to measure cluster compactness in embedding space analysis.

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Regularization-based:** LwF (with Teacher Adaptation), LGKD, SDCOT, 3DPC-CISS.
    *   **Optimization-based:** C-FSCIL.
    *   **DGCNN-specific comparisons:** BiDist, CLOM, TEEN, FACT, ALICE.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Backbone Architectures:** PointTransformer (primary), DGCNN (secondary/model-agnostic validation).
    *   **Hyperbolic Space:** Poincaré ball model with curvature $c = -1.0$.
    *   **Optimizer:** Riemannian SGD (facilitated by `geoopt` for hyperbolic operations) and AdamW.
    *   **Batch Size:** 16.
    *   **Learning Rate:** Initial learning rate of 0.001.
    *   **Weight Decay:** 0.0001.
    *   **Training Duration:** 100 epochs.
    *   **Text Embeddings:** CLIP frozen text encoder used to obtain semantic embeddings for Ideal Prototypes initialization.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Embedding Space Analysis:**
*   We visualized the embedding space using UMAP projections of the Poincaré ball to 2D for the S3DIS dataset.
*   Observation: The hyperbolic space's negative curvature enabled a more compact representation and clearer class separation compared to Euclidean space.
*   Quantitative Evidence of Compactness: The Dunn index (higher is better) for HiPo was **0.69**, whereas for Euclidean space it was **0.35**.

**Qualitative Segmentation Performance:**
*   We compared segmentation visualizations on the S3DIS dataset against baselines like SDCOT and 3DPC-CISS.
*   Observation: Even in few-shot setups, HiPo successfully segmented small and challenging parts (e.g., walls, counters) where other baselines struggled or failed.

**Sensitivity to Shot Count (Data Availability):**
*   We analyzed the effect of increasing training samples per class (from 1-shot to Full-data) on the 10-2T setting.
*   Observation: Catastrophic forgetting was most severe with limited data.
*   Observation: Increasing the number of training examples significantly mitigated forgetting for HiPo, whereas it exacerbated forgetting for the baseline SDCOT.
*   Observation: HiPo outperformed the top-2 baseline methods in terms of Last mIoU and forgetting mitigation in the 10-2T setting.

**Ablation Findings:**
*   **Penalty $\phi$ (Busemann Loss):** We observed that without a penalty ($\phi=0$), samples were overly drawn to Ideal Prototypes, causing overconfident predictions, vanishing gradients, and lower AIA. Conversely, a high penalty ($\phi=1$) increased inter-class confusion. The optimal balance was typically found between 0.25 and 0.75.
*   **Curvature:** We found that a negative curvature ($c=-1.00$) consistently outperformed small positive/zero curvatures ($c=0.0001$, approximating Euclidean space). This confirmed that Riemannian geometry captured the hierarchical structure of point clouds more effectively than Euclidean space.
*   **Backbone Agnosticism:** While many SOTA methods performed well with DGCNN but degraded with PointTransformer, HiPo remained effective across both architectures, demonstrating it is model-agnostic.

# CVPR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the latex paper writing process for CVPR 2025.

## Language
All manuscripts must be in English.

## Submission Policies & Anonymity
CVPR reviewing is double-blind. Authors must not know the names of the reviewers, and reviewers must not know the names of the authors.

* **No Identifying Information:** Do not provide information that may identify the authors in the acknowledgments (e.g., co-workers and grant IDs) or in the supplementary material.
* **Links:** Do not provide links to websites that identify the authors.
* **GitHub:** Links to GitHub must be anonymous.
* **Self-Citation:** If you need to cite any of your own papers that are being submitted concurrently, include anonymized versions in the supplementary material and cite them as anonymous. Do not use the words "my" or "our" when citing previous work; treat your own prior work as if it were written by someone else (e.g., "Smith et al. showed..." rather than "We showed...").

## Paper length
Papers, excluding the references section, must be no longer than eight pages in length.
The references section will not be included in the page count, and there is no limit on the length of the references section.
For example, a paper of eight pages with two pages of references would have a total length of 10 pages.

Overlength papers, or papers where margins and formatting are deemed significantly altered, will simply not be reviewed.

## Mathematics
Please number all of your sections and displayed equations as in these examples:
```latex
\begin{equation}
  E = m\cdot c^2
  \label{eq:important}
\end{equation}
```
and
```latex
\begin{equation}
  v = a\cdot t.
  \label{eq:also-important}
\end{equation}
```

## Formatting your paper
All text must be in a two-column format.
The total allowable size of the text area is $6\frac78$ inches (17.46 cm) wide by $8\frac78$ inches (22.54 cm) high.
Columns are to be $3\frac14$ inches (8.25 cm) wide, with a $\frac{5}{16}$ inch (0.8 cm) space between them.
The main title (on the first page) should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge of the page.
The second and following pages should begin 1 inch (2.54 cm) from the top edge.
On all pages, the bottom margin should be $1\frac{1}{8}$ inches (2.86 cm) from the bottom edge of the page for $8.5 \times 11$-inch paper;
for A4 paper, approximately $1\frac{5}{8}$ inches (4.13 cm) from the bottom edge of the page.

### Type style and fonts
Wherever Times is specified, Times Roman may also be used. If neither is available on your word processor, please use the font closest in appearance to Times to which you have access.

### Main Title
Center the title $1\frac{3}{8}$ inches (3.49 cm) from the top edge of the first page. The title should be in Times 14-point, boldface type. Capitalize the first letter of nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs; do not capitalize articles, coordinate conjunctions, or prepositions (unless the title begins with such a word).

The ABSTRACT and MAIN TEXT are to be in a two-column format.

### Main Text
Type main text in 10-point Times, single-spaced.
Do NOT use double-spacing.
All paragraphs should be indented 1 pica (approx.~$\frac{1}{6}$ inch or 0.422 cm). Make sure your text is fully justified---that is, flush left and flush right. Please do not place any additional blank lines between paragraphs.

Figure and table captions should be 9-point Roman type as in \cref{fig:onecol,fig:short}. 
Short captions should be centred.

\noindent Callouts should be 9-point Helvetica, non-boldface type. Initially capitalize only the first word of section titles and first-, second-, and third-order headings.

#### First-order Headings
For example, {\large \bf 1. Introduction} should be Times 12-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one blank line after.

#### Second-order Headings
For example, { \bf 1.1. Database elements} should be Times 11-point boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, with one blank line before, and one after.
If you require a third-order heading (we discourage it), use 10-point Times, boldface, initially capitalized, flush left, preceded by one blank line, followed by a period and your text on the same line.

### Footnotes
Please use \footnote{This is what a footnote looks like.
It often distracts the reader from the main flow of the argument.} sparingly.

Indeed, try to avoid footnotes altogether and include necessary peripheral observations in the text (within parentheses, if you prefer, as in this sentence). If you wish to use a footnote, place it at the bottom of the column on the page on which it is referenced.
Use Times 8-point type, single-spaced.

### Cross-references

```latex
{\small\begin{verbatim}
  \cref{...}
\end{verbatim}}
```
command for cross-referencing to figures, tables, equations, or sections.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

We address the challenge of **Few-Shot Class Incremental Learning (FSCIL)** within the domain of **3D point cloud semantic segmentation**. Conventional supervised segmentation methods rely on static, large-scale labeled datasets and a fixed label set. However, real-world applications (such as robotics and autonomous systems) operate in dynamic environments where novel object categories emerge sequentially. The system must learn these new classes with limited supervision (few-shot) without erasing the representations of previously learned classes (catastrophic forgetting).

A critical technical gap exists in how current methods represent the complex, hierarchical structure of 3D point cloud data. Existing FSCIL approaches predominantly rely on **Euclidean embeddings**. Euclidean space suffers from limited capacity and high distortion when modeling hierarchical data, leading to "compaction" where new class embeddings encroach upon existing ones. This exacerbates the **stability-plasticity trade-off**, causing severe overfitting to new, scarce data and interference with old memories. Furthermore, standard optimization in alternative geometries (like hyperbolic space) often encounters vanishing gradient problems when embeddings approach the boundary, making them unstable for incremental learning tasks.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose a framework named **Hyperbolic Ideal Prototypes Optimization (HiPo)**. Our central hypothesis is that the **Poincaré Hyperbolic Sphere** ($\mathbb{B}_c^n$) is the mathematically optimal embedding manifold for 3D point clouds due to its negative curvature and exponential volume growth, which naturally mirrors the tree-like, hierarchical nature of 3D data.

We hypothesize that by anchoring class representations to **Ideal Prototypes** fixed at the "infinity" boundary of the Poincaré ball, we can maintain a stable classifier structure that resists drift during incremental updates. By enriching these prototypes with semantic information (via CLIP) and optimizing them via a modified **Busemann loss function** (which handles distances to infinity) combined with an uncertainty-aware regularization term, we can maximize class separability and minimize the interference typically seen in Euclidean FSCIL.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will define the learning process as a sequence of sessions $\{ S^{(0)}, \dots, S^{(T)} \}$. The base session $S^{(0)}$ contains abundant samples, while subsequent sessions $S^{(t)}$ ($t > 0$) provide $N$-way $K$-shot labeled point clouds for disjoint new classes.

### 1. Geometric Embedding Space
We will utilize the **Poincaré ball model** of hyperbolic geometry. We define the manifold $\mathbb{B}_c^n = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n : c \|x\|^2 < 1 \}$ with negative curvature $c$. This space allows for exponentially increasing volume as we move away from the origin, providing sufficient capacity to accommodate incremental classes with minimal distortion.

### 2. Hyperbolic Ideal Prototype Positioning
Unlike standard methods that learn prototypes dynamically, we will pre-assign **Ideal Prototypes** on the boundary of the Poincaré ball (points at infinity). Let $u_1, \dots, u_n$ be the prototypes for $n$ classes. They will reside on the boundary $\mathcal{T}_n$:
$$ \mathcal{T}_n = \{ u \in \mathbb{R}^n : \|u\|^2 = 1 \} $$
To ensure these prototypes carry semantic meaning, we will utilize a frozen **CLIP text encoder**. For each class, we extract text embeddings $S = \{ s_1, \dots, s_n \}$. We will then optimize the positions of the Ideal Prototypes $u$ to reflect the semantic similarity in $S$ while enforcing orthogonality to maximize separability.

We formulate a **Hyperbolic Positioning Loss** ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HIP}}$), inspired by ranking objectives, to optimize prototype placement:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HIP}} = \frac { 1 } { | M | } \sum _ { ( i , i ^ { \prime } , i ^ { \prime \prime } ) \in M } - \bar { W } _ { i i ^ { \prime } i ^ { \prime \prime } } \log W _ { i i ^ { \prime } i ^ { \prime \prime } } $$
Here, $M$ is the set of class triplets. The ranking order $\bar { W } _ { i i ^ { \prime } i ^ { \prime \prime } }$ is determined by the cosine similarity of the CLIP embeddings $s$. The term $W _ { i i ^ { \prime } i ^ { \prime \prime } }$ is the probability derived from the hyperbolic alignment of prototypes $u$:
$$ W_{ii'i''} = \frac{e^{\mathcal{O}_{ii'i''}}}{1 + e^{\mathcal{O}_{ii'i''}}}, \quad \text{where} \quad \mathcal{O}_{ii'i''} = \cos \theta_{u_i, u_{i'}} - \cos \theta_{u_i, u_{i''}} $$
This ensures that if class $i$ is semantically closer to $i'$ than to $i''$, their hyperbolic prototypes will structurally reflect this hierarchy.

### 3. Architecture and Hyperbolic Projection
Our backbone will be a **PointTransformer** feature extractor $\mathcal{E}(.)$. Since computing Fréchet means directly in hyperbolic space is computationally expensive, we will compute class prototypes in Euclidean space and project them.
1.  **Extraction:** For an input point cloud $P_k^{(t)}$, we extract Euclidean features $v_k^{(t)} = \mathcal{E}(P_k^{(t)})$.
2.  **Averaging:** We compute the mean feature vector $\bar{v}(c_i^{(t)})$ for class $c_i^{(t)}$ in Euclidean space.
3.  **Projection:** We project this mean into the Poincaré ball using the exponential map $\exp_0(.)$ and a **Möbius layer** (hyperbolic feed-forward layer) $\mathcal{M}$:
$$ z(c_i^{(t)}) = \mathcal{M} ( \exp_0 ( \bar{v}(c_i^{(t)}) ) ) $$
Here, $z(c_i^{(t)})$ is the learned hyperbolic prototype for the class.

### 4. Loss Formulation: Uncertainty-Aware Busemann Learning
To train the network, we must measure the distance between the learned embedding $z_i^t$ and the fixed Ideal Prototype $u_i^t$ at infinity. Standard geodesic distance is undefined for points at infinity. Therefore, we will employ the **Busemann function** $\mathcal{B}$.

The Busemann distance from an embedding $z_i^t$ to an ideal prototype $u_i^t$ in the Poincaré ball is formulated as:
$$ \mathcal{B}_{u_i^t} ( z_i^t ) = \log \frac { \| u_i^t - z_i^t \| ^ 2 } { 1 - \| z_i^t \| ^ 2 } $$
This acts as our primary alignment term, pulling features toward their class-specific direction at infinity.

To prevent overfitting (feature collapse) and vanishing gradients near the boundary, we introduce an **Uncertainty-Aware Regularization** term. We use the hyperbolic distance from the origin $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{B}}$ as a proxy for uncertainty. The alignment loss is defined as:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Alignment}} = \mathcal{B}_{u_i^t} ( z_i^t ) + \phi \cdot d_{\mathbb{B}} ( z_i^t , \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{B}} ) $$
where $\phi$ is a regularization hyperparameter. This penalty prevents embeddings from drifting too close to the boundary (high uncertainty) prematurely.

The final objective function for training combines the alignment loss with a standard Cross-Entropy loss ($\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}$) for the point-level classification branch:
$$ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{HIPo}} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Alignment}} + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} $$

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Theoretical Advancement:** We will demonstrate that hyperbolic geometry significantly reduces distortion for hierarchical 3D data compared to Euclidean spaces, theoretically validating the use of the Poincaré ball for point cloud segmentation.
2.  **Architectural Novelty:** The introduction of **HiPo** will be the first framework to integrate fixed Ideal Prototypes with CLIP-derived semantics and Busemann optimization specifically for the 3D FSCIL domain.
3.  **Robustness:** By enforcing orthogonality at the hyperbolic boundary and penalizing uncertainty, we expect to decouple the stability-plasticity trade-off, allowing the model to assimilate new classes without the catastrophic forgetting characteristic of current state-of-the-art methods.

network.web_access: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.
notes.search: Provider server-side web search is switched off in every sibling by the agent CLIs' own system settings, bind-mounted read-only by the docker shim: Claude Code /etc/claude-code/managed-settings.json (permissions.deny WebSearch), Codex /etc/codex/config.toml (web_search="disabled") and /etc/codex/requirements.toml (allowed_web_search_modes=["disabled"]). notes.key_exposure: The provider key is in the environment of the agent containers (upstream env-file mechanism) and therefore visible to commands the agent runs. Claude Code's CLAUDE_CODE_SUBPROCESS_ENV_SCRUB=1 was tried and aborts: it needs bubblewrap, which the unmodified upstream agent image lacks.
notes.gpu: gpus=1 is wired (container.gpu_count, harness GPU evaluation) but was not exercised.
notes.docker_socket: The orchestrator container has the host docker socket (root-equivalent on the host).

network.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

agent.how: no external coding agent: EvoScientist's in-process sub-agents (LangChain deepagents)

tools.permissions: think_tool, deepagents built-ins, EvoSkills skills and an execute shell; skill_manager not registered; no search tool

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
